title: Manoj Kumar vs Naval Kishore on 27 October, 2018
full_text: Manoj Kumar vs Naval Kishore on 27 October, 2018 IN THE COURT OF MS. PRIYANKA RAJPOOT, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE, NORTH-WEST, ROHINI, DELHI CC No. 4141/2016 Manoj Kumar S/o Late Sh. Kaptan Singh R/o H.No. 29, Village Pooth Kalan, Delhi-110086 ............Complainant Versus Naval Kishore S/o Sh. Mool Chand R/o H.No. 17/656, Bank Enclave, Bahadurgarh, Haryana. Office address : State Bank of Patiala Single Window Operator, Pooth Kalan, Kanjhawla Road, New Delhi-110086 .............Accused JUDGMENT (1) Name of the complainant, : Manoj Kumar parentage and address S/o Late Sh. Kaptan Singh R/o H.No. 29, Village Pooth Kalan, Delhi-110086 (2) Name of accused, : Naval Kishore parentage and address S/o Sh. Mool Chand R/o H.No. 17/656, Bank Enclave, Bahadurgarh, Haryana. Office address : State Bank of Patiala Single Window Operator, Pooth Kalan, Kanjhawla Road, New Delhi-110086 (3) Offence complained of or proved : 138 N.I. Act (4) Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty (5) Date of institution of case : 01.05.2012 Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 1 (6) Date of reserve of order : 20.10.2018 (7) Date of Final Order : 26.10.2018 (8) Final Order : Convicted 1. Vide this judgment I shall dispose of the complaint filed by the complainant under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act '). 2. Brief facts relevant for the decision of the case are as under:- That the complainant was having good friendly relations with one Sh. Naveen Solanki who introduced the accused with the complainant. In the month of November 2010, the accused alongwith Sh. Naveen Solanki approached the complainant for a friendly loan of Rs.3,50,000/- as he was facing financial crises. On repeated requests, the complainant advanced the said amount to the accused and one agreement was also executed in this regard. The accused agreed to pay within six months i.e. in between 18.11.2010 to 17.05.2011. After the expiry of stipulated period, the complainant contacted the accused who issued a cheque bearing no. 170464 dated 30.01.2012 for a sum of Rs.3,50,000/- drawn on State Bank of Patiala, Poothkalan, Block Kanjhawala Road, New Delhi, in discharge of his liability. On presentation, the said cheque was returned unpaid with the remarks "funds insufficient" vide returning memo dated 10.03.2012. The complainant issued a legal notice dated 19.03.2012 through his counsel by registered A.D. as well as UPC. The legal notice was duly served upon the accused. However, the accused neither replied to the notice nor made any payment. Thereafter, complainant has filed the present complaint case with the submission that accused be summoned, tried and punished according to law. 3. In his pre-summoning evidence, complainant examined himself on affidavit Ex. CW-1/1. He reiterated the contents of complaint and placed on record, cheque bearing no. 170464 dated 30.01.2012 for a sum of Rs.3,50,000/- drawn on State Bank of Patiala, Poothkalan, Block Kanjhawala Road, New Delhi as Ex. CW1/A, cheque returning memo dated 10.03.2012 as Ex. CW-1/B, legal notice dated 19.03.2012 as Ex. CW-1/C, postal receipts as Ex. CW-1/E & Ex. CW-1/E1, tracking reports as Ex. CW-1/D & Ex. CW-1/D1 and loan agreement as Ex. CW-1/X. 4. Upon appreciation of pre-summoning evidence, accused was summoned for an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Act and notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. for this offence Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 2 was framed upon accused on 03.07.2013 to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. He stated that he had given undated cheque to the complainant on request of the complainant for showing to some other person. He denied receiving of legal notice. He denied having any liability towards the complainant. He also stated that he had settled the matter with the complainant as he was his friend. 5. Thereafter, the complainant was examined, cross-examined and discharged. During cross-examination, the complainant stated that he met the accused through Sh. Naveen Solanki who is his nephew. He stated that he has given friendly loan to the accused. He stated that on 17.11.2010, he refused to give loan to the accused when he came along with Sh. Naveen Solanki for the first time. He stated that on the next day i.e. 18.11.2010, both of them had come again he had given loan of Rs.3,50,000/- to the accused by way of FDR of Rs.3,00,000/- and Rs.50,000/- in cash. He stated that he gave authority to the accused to encash the FDR as he was working in the same bank i.e. State Bank of Patiala. He stated that he had given the loan amount without interest. He stated that loan agreement Ex. CW-1/X was executed between him and the accused at his residence in the presence of Sh. Naveen Solanki but he was not witness to the agreement. He stated that the loan was given for a period of six months and the accused had given undated cheque. He volunteered to state that the accused asked him to fill the date in the cheque on his instructions. He stated that his brother Sh. Sandeep Solanki has mentioned the date in the cheque in question. He admitted that there is an over writing on Ex. CW-1/A. He stated that the contents in the cheque in question except the date are in the handwriting of the accused. He denied the suggestion that he had given a loan of Rs.1,00,000/- only on interest at the rate of 10% per month to the accused. He denied the suggestion that the accused has given the cheque in question as security in a blank signed manner. He denied the suggestion that he has misused the security cheque of the accused by filing the present case. He stated that the accused has agreed to pay loan amount on or before 17.05.2011. He admitted that he has not taken any legal action against the accused for recovery of loan amount from 17.05.2011 to January 2012. He stated that he presented the cheque in question in his bank on 30.01.2012. He denied the suggestion that the cheque in question was never presented in his bank for encashment. He stated that after the cheque in question was dishonoured on 07.02.2012, he did not send any legal notice to the accused. He could not recall the date and month when he presented the cheque in question for second time. He stated that even thereafter he did not initiate any legal action against the accused. He stated that when the cheque in question was dishonoured for the third time, he initiated legal action against the accused. He denied the suggestion that the cheque in question was never presented in the bank. He denied the suggestion that legal notice was not delivered to the Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 3 accused as the same was not sent to him. He denied the suggestion that the agreement as well as the cheque were signed by the accused as security. He denied the suggestion that he had not initiated legal action against the accused as he had been receiving interest of Rs.10,000/- per month from the accused on principal amount of Rs.1,00,000/-. He denied the suggestion that the accused stopped giving him interest from January 2012 onwards and therefore, he has misused the cheque in question which was given to him as security. He denied the suggestion that Sh. Naveen Solanki has nothing to do with the transaction that took place with the accused as he was not present at the time of transaction. He stated that the accused has issued the cheque in question on 18.11.2010 when the loan of Rs.3,50,000/- was given to him. He stated that at the time of execution of agreement, Sh. Sandeep Solanki was also present at his house. He denied the suggestion that Ex. CW-1/D, Ex. CW-1/D1, Ex. CW-1/E & Ex. CW-1/E1 are false and fabricated documents. He denied the suggestion that he has filed the false case. 6. On 29.05.2015, statement of accused under Section 281 Cr.P.C. read with Section 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded in which all the incriminating evidence were put to him to which accused stated that he never took loan of Rs.3,50,000/- from the complainant. He further stated that loan agreement Ex. CW-1/X was not executed between them. He further stated that he signed the loan agreement as Sh. Sandeep Solanki asked him to sign the same at the time of taking loan from him. He further stated that he had given ten cheques cheque in question to Sh. Sandeep Solanki for taking of loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from him. He admitted the signature on the cheque in question, however, denied having filled in contents therein. He denied receiving of legal notice. He stated that he does not have any liability towards the complainant. The accused preferred to lead defence evidence. 7. In defence evidence, the accused has examined himself as DW-1. He deposed that he took a loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from Sh. Sandeep Solanki in the month of November 2010 at the rate of 10% per month. He also stated that he knew the complainant and his brother as they used to come in his bank i.e. State Bank of Patiala. He also stated that there was no friendly relations with the complainant and his brother. He also stated that the complainant is a financier by profession and he used to give loan at heavy rate of interest to the customers. He also stated that he handed over 10 blank signed cheques and various documents to Sh. Sandeep Solanki at the time of taking loan from him. He also stated that as per the directions of Sh. Sandeep Solanki, he used to give Rs.10,000/- per month to him or to any other person including his brother namely Sh. Manoj. He also stated that in the month of December 2010 and January 2011, he had transferred Rs.1,000/- in the account of Sh. Sandeep Solanki and Rs.9,000/- in the account of Sh. Manoj. He also stated that in the month of February 2011, he had Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 4 transferred Rs.10,000/- each to the account of Sh. Sandeep Solanki and Sh. Manoj. He also stated that during the present proceedings, he had given Rs.40,000/- to the complainant. He also stated that he had returned the entire loan amount with interest to Sh. Sandeep Solanki. He also stated that he does not owe any amount towards Sh. Manoj Kumar as he had not taken any loan from him. He also stated that Sh. Sandeep Solanki and Sh. Manoj Kumar have misused his blank signed cheques and blank signed documents which were given at the time of advancement of loan. He also stated that the cheques were given as security for loan of Rs.1,00,000/- which had already been paid to Sh. Sandeep Solanki. He denied receiving of legal notice. He also stated that the cheques were never presented in his account. During his cross-examination, he stated that he was working in the bank as Single Window Operator. He stated that no agreement was executed between him and Sh.Sandeep Solanki at the time of taking of loan. He denied the suggestion that at the instance of Sh. Naveen Solanki, he had taken loan from Sh. Sandeep Solanki and Sh. Manoj Kumar. He denied the suggestion that the contents in the cheque in question were filled by him. He also stated that he has not filed any document to show that the complainant is a financier by profession. He also stated that he has not filed any document which can show that he has taken loan of Rs.1,00,000/- at the rate of interest of 10% per month. He also stated that he has not filed any document regarding transfer of amount in the bank account of Sh. Sandeep Solanki and Sh. Manoj Kumar in the month of December 2010, January & February 2011. He denied the suggestion that he had taken a loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from Sh. Sandeep Solanki. He denied the suggestion that he had taken Rs.3,50,000/- from Sh. Manoj Kumar. He stated that he has not filed any police complaint regarding misusing of his cheques. He denied the suggestion that he has received the legal notice. He denied the suggestion that the cheques were given to the complainant for security. 8. Final arguments were addressed on behalf of both the parties. Thereafter, the matter was listed for orders. In the mean time, the complainant moved an application under Section 311 Cr.P.C. for summoning the bank witness. The application was allowed by the court vide order dated 05.09.2017. In pursuant to his application, the bank witness was summmoned. On 06.12.2017, one Sh. Naveen Katyal, witness from State Bank of India(previously known as State Bank of Patiala), Kanjhawala Branch, Delhi, had appeared and he was examined by the complainant and the cross-examination was deferred as the Ld. Counsel for the accused was not feeling well. Thereafter, on the next date of hearing i.e. 24.01.2018, the bank had sent another person namely Ms. Poonam as Sh. Naveen Katyal was transferred from the bank. Ms. Poonam as CW-3 was examined by the complainant. She deposed that Sh. Manoj Kumar i.e. the complainant has presented the cheque in question which was returned at the counter due to Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 5 "insufficient funds" on 10.03.2012. She has placed on record one document i.e. cheque return record Ex. CW-3/1. During her cross-examination, she stated that the cheque is endorsed by the bank on the back side before its presentation for encashment. She also stated that sometimes cheques are presented without any endorsement or stamp of the bank on its back side. She admitted that in case if the cheque is dishonoured, debit charges are deducted from the account of payee. She also stated that she does not know who has signed Ex. CW-1/B. She denied the suggestion that the charges were not deducted from the account of the accused as Ex. CW-1/A was never presented in the bank and it was not dishonoured. She also stated that the charges are deducted only when the cheque of some other bank is put for clearance. She denied the suggestion that she is giving the statement in connivance with complainant. With the permission of the court, she was re-examined by Ld. Counsel for the complainant. She stated that the bank do not put any endorsement on the cheque before clearance, if the drawer and drawee of the cheque are having account in the same bank. 9. While drafting the judgment, it came into the notice of undersigned that Ex. CW-3/D1 was not there in the judicial file. The court invoked its power under Section 311 of Cr.P.C. and summoned the bank witness for placing on record the statement of account of the accused. In pursuant the said order, Ms. Poonam, from State Bank of India, Pooth Kalan Branch had appeared. She was examined as a court witness. She placed on record statement of account of accused Ex. SW/A for the period 30.01.2012 to 31.12.2012, statement of overdraft account of the accused Ex. SW/D for the period 01.01.2012 to 01.06.2015, certificate under Section 2(b) and 2 A (c) of the Banker's Book of Evidence Act, 1891 Ex. SW/C and Certificate under Section 65B of Indian Evidence Act Ex. SW/B. During her cross-examination, she stated that the cheque in question is not reflected in the statement of account of the accused Ex. SW/D. She admitted that cheque bounce charges were not deducted from the account of the accused. She admitted that Ex. CW-1/A is a bearer cheque. She denied the suggested that a bearer cheque can be encashed by any person even though his name is not mentioned in the cheque. 10. I have considered the rival submissions of the parties and perused the entire evidence led by the complainant as well as by the accused. 11. Before appreciating the facts of the case in detail for the purpose of decision, let relevant position of law be discussed first:- For the offence under Section 138 of the Act to be made out against the accused, the complainant must prove the following points, that:- 1. the accused issued a cheque on account maintained by him with a bank. Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 6 2. the said cheque has been issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of any legal debt or other liability. 3. the said cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date of cheque or within the period of its validity. 4. the aforesaid cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned unpaid/dishonoured. 5. the payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand to the drawer within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque. 6. the drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of aforesaid legal notice of demand. 12. The Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque i.e. complainant in the present case; firstly, in regard to the passing of consideration as contained in Section 118 (a) and secondly, a presumption that the holder of cheque receiving the same of the nature referred to in Section 139 discharged in whole or in part any debt or other liability. Section 118 of the N.I Act provides : "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration - that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows: "Presumption in favour of holder - it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability". 13. For the offence under Section 138 of the Act, the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 have to be compulsory raised as soon as execution of cheque by accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter burden is shifted to accused to prove otherwise. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. A presumption is not in itself evidence but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. Presumptions both under Sections 118 and 139 are rebuttable in nature. Same was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee [(2001) 6 SCC 16]. 14. It has been held in M/s. Kumar Exports v. M/s. Sharma Carpets, [2009 A.I.R. (SC) Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 7 1518] that the accused may rebut these presumptions by leading direct evidence and in some and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial. Further, the burden may be discharged by the accused by showing preponderance of probabilities and the onus on the accused is not as heavy as it is on the complainant to prove his case. 15. In the present case, the accused has admitted in the notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. that the cheque in question bears his signature and he issued the same in favour of the complainant. Reference can be made to Judgment of Apex Court in Rangappa v. Mohan , AIR 2010 SC 1898,that, "Once the cheque relates to the account of the accused and he accepts and admits the signatures on the said cheque, then initial presumption as contemplated under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act has to be raised by the Court in favour of the complainant." 16. It means that in the present case the onus is upon the accused to rebut the presumption raised under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the said Act and merely saying that the cheque in question was given by him to the complainant as security cheque is not sufficient to rebut the presumption. 17. The first defence taken by the accused that he has not received the legal notice. During the trial, accused has never challenged about the correctness of his address. He merely stated that it was not delivered to him. In such cases, sending of notice at the correct address is sufficient. It is not necessary that the notice must be received by the drawer of the cheque. The accused challenged the fact of non receipt of notice, however, he did not bring any cogent evidence showing non delivery of the same. The legal notice having been dispatched by Registered Post, there arose a presumption of due service as per Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 18971 and Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 2 and now it was incumbent on the accused to lead evidence to prove that the same was not served on him. No evidence has been led to rebut the presumption of deemed service. In such circumstances, the legal notice can be presumed to have been served. 1 Section 27 : Where any (Central Act) or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes of requires any document to be served by post, where the expression any other expression in used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing pre-paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. 2 Section 114 : The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particulars case. Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 8 For this, I rely upon the case of D. Vinod Shivapa v. Nanda Belliappa , 2006 (6) SCC 456, wherein it was held that when a notice is sent by the registered post and is returned with the postal endorsement 'refused' or 'unclaimed' or 'not available in the house' or 'house locked' or 'shop closed' or 'addressee not in station', due service has to be presumed. The question as to whether the service of notice has been fraudulently refused by unscrupulous means is as question of fact to be decided on the basis of evidence. In the case of C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. 2007 (2) JCC (NI) 225, it was held that any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within fifteen days of receipt of summons from the Court for complaint filed under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of cheque amount and makes submission to this effect before the Court and accordingly, the complaint is liable to be rejected. Where no payment is made under the above circumstances, such person can not contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 of the Act, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of The General Clauses Act and Section 114 of The Evidence Act. In view of the said interpretation, deemed service is to be accepted by the Court unless it is rebutted by leading cogent evidence. 18. The accused has taken the defence that he has not taken any loan from the complainant. He alleged that he has taken loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from one Sh. Sandeep Solanki in November 2010 at the rate of 10% per month and at the time of taking of loan, he issued 10 blank signed cheques and various documents to him. He also alleged that he used to pay Rs.10,000/- per month to Sh. Sandeep Solanki or to other persons including his brother i.e. the complainant at the instance of Sh. Sandeep Solanki. However, no cogent evidence has been adduced by the accused in support of his version. During cross-examination, the accused has admitted that he has not placed on record any document to show that he has transferred the amount to the bank account of complainant and his brother Sh. Sandeep Solanki. In the absence of documentary evidence, testimony of accused can not be relied upon. 19. It is worth mentioning here that the accused has taken inconsistent stand at different stages. At the time of framing of notice, he stated that he had given undated cheque to the complainant on his request for showing it to some other person and that he had settled the matter with the complainant as he was his friend whereas during cross-examination of the complainant, Ld. Counsel for the accused has given the suggestion to him that he has given loan of Rs.1,00,000/- on 10% interest to the accused. It was also suggested to him that the cheque in question was given as security in a blank signed manner. At the stage of recording of statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. and defence evidence, the accused stated that he never took loan of Rs.3,50,000/- from the complainant and the cheque in question was given to Sh. Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 9 Sandeep Solanki against loan of Rs.1,00,000/-. Thus, the contradictory stand taken by the accused at different stages is sufficient to infer that he has failed to rebut the presumption of legal liability. Furthermore, the complainant has placed on record loan agreement Ex. CW-1/X in support of his claim. Ex. CW-1/X acknowledges debt of Rs.3,50,000/- owed by the accused in favour of the complainant. The accused has admitted his signatures on the agreement but he has claimed that it was not executed between him and the complainant. It can be inferred from the suggestion put to the complainant during his cross-examination that nowhere it was asked whether Ex. CW-1/X was executed between Sh. Sandeep Solanki and the accused and not between accused and the complainant. The complainant during his cross-examination, stated that the said agreement was executed between him and the complainant at his residence. At this juncture, it is pertinent to note that Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act and states that : Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement.- When the terms of any such contract, grant or other disposition of property, or any matter required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, have been proved according to the last section, no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted, as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest, for the purpose of contradicting, varying , adding to, or subtracting from, its terms. The fact alleged by the accused is not covered in any proviso to the said section. Therefore, considering the existence of loan agreement between the parties, no oral statement regarding the agreement is admissible. The accused can not dispute the agreement Ex. CW-1/X by alleging that he has not taken Rs.3,50,000/- from the complainant. 20. Furthermore, if the case of the accused is that the entire amount had already been repaid and nothing is due from him to the complainant or his brother Sandeep Solanki, he should have either given reply to the legal notice or file police complaint against them. It has been observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in V.S Yadav v. Reena , [172(2010)DLT 561] as under: "Mere pleading not guilty and stating that the cheques were issued as security, would not give amount to rebutting the presumption raised under Section 139 of N.I. Act. If mere statement under Section 313 Cr. P.C. or under Section 281 Cr. P.C. of accused of pleading not guilty was sufficient to rebut the entire evidence produced by the complainant/ prosecution, then every accused has to be acquitted. But, it is not the law. In order to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of N.I. Act, the accused, by cogent evidence, has to prove the circumstance under which cheques were issued. It was for the accused to prove if no loan was taken why he did not write a letter to the complainant for return of the cheque. Unless the accused had proved that he acted like a normal businessman/prudent person entering into a contract he could not have rebutted the presumption u/s 139 N.I. Act. If no loan was given, but cheques were retained, he Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 10 immediately would have protested and asked the cheques to be returned and if still cheques were not returned, he would have served a notice as complainant. Nothing was proved in this case.'' In the present case, the accused during his cross-examination, has admitted that he has not filed any complaint before the police against the complainant regarding misuse of cheque in question as well as blank signed documents. Thus, the bald plea of the accused having not been substantiated by cogent evidence is not reliable. 21. The accused has also taken the defence that the cheque in question was never presented in the bank and thus, one of the mandatory requirement of 138 of the Act is not fulfilled. It was argued by Ld. Counsel for the accused that as per the guidelines of Reserve Bank of India, banks are required to put seal of the bank on the cheque whenever it is presented and if it gets dishonoured, charges have to be deducted from the account of the drawer. It was also argued by him that the statement of account of the accused Ex. SW/D does not indicate or suggest that the cheque in question has been presented or the same has been dishonoured since no amount has been deducted from the account of the accused for dishonour of the cheque and thus, it proves that the cheque was never presented by the complainant. It was also argued that the cheque in question is a bearer cheque which can be presented and returned at the counter of the bank and thus, section 138 of the Act will not apply to the bearer cheque. I do not find any substance in the submission of Ld. Counsel for the accused. The cheques are basically of two types. A bearer cheque or a crossed cheque. A bearer cheques can be encashed across the counter in the bank without routing it through any bank account. Section 138 of the Act states that where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence. Thus, the section does not distinguish between bearer cheque and account payee cheque. Section 142(2)(b) states that if the cheque is presented for payment by the payee or holder in due course, otherwise through an account, the branch of the drawee bank where the drawer maintains the account, is situated. Thus, it shows that section 138 of the Act is applicable to the bearer cheque as well. Ld. Counsel for the accused has failed to show any authority or provision of law which shows that Section 138 of the Act will apply only to account payee cheques and not to bearer cheques. The complainant has placed on record returning memo dated 10.03.2012 Ex. CW-1/B which shows that the cheque Ex. CW-1/A was returned unpaid for the reasons "funds insufficient". Ex. CW-1/B bears the signature of the officer of the drawee Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 11 bank. Merely because the charges for dishonour are not deducted, it can not be presumed that the cheque has not been presented. If there is any lapse on the part of drawee bank in not deducting charges for dishonour, it would not absolve the drawer from the liability which flows from dishonour of cheque. The complainant has examined bank official to prove that the cheque in question was presented and it was dishonoured. Bank witness namely Ms. Poonam CW-3 has placed on record cheque return register Ex. CW-3/1 which shows that the cheque in question was returned on 10.03.2012. Thus, the factum of dishonour of cheque is duly proved by the complainant. 22. In view of the above, this court is of the considered opinion that the accused has failed to rebut the presumption in favour of complainant either on the basis of material available on record or by adducing any defence evidence. The complainant has led cogent evidence to prove his case. Therefore, complainant has successfully proved his case beyond reasonable doubt. 23. As the complainant has proved his case beyond reasonable doubt, therefore, accused is being convicted for the offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 24. Let the accused be heard on quantum of sentence. 25. Copy of Judgment be supplied to the convict free of cost. Digitally signed by PRIYANKA PRIYANKA RAJPOOT RAJPOOT Date: 2018.10.27 18:06:29 +0530 ANNOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT (PRIYANKA RAJPOOT) TODAY i.e. 26th OCTOBER 2018 METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE ROHINI DISTRICT COURTS/ DELHI Manoj Kumar v. Naval Kishore 27.10.2018 ORDER ON SENTENCE Present: Complainant with Ld. Proxy Counsel Sh. Tarun Upadhayey. Convict with Ld. counsel Sh. Satish Kumar. Arguments heard on the point on sentence. It is stated by Ld. Counsel for the convict that convict is senior citizen and is having family consisting of his wife. It is further submitted that he has retired and he is getting Rs.24,000/- as pension. Ld. Counsel for the convict requests the court to take lenient view against the convict. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that the matter pertains to the year 2012 and relates to loan transaction and the convict has defrauded the complainant and several other persons. I have heard the submissions and carefully perused the record. Complaint regarding present cheque in question is pending since 2012 and the same relates to loan transaction between the parties. I am not inclined to grant the benefit of Probation of Offenders Act as the matter pertains to the year 2012 and cheque bouncing cases are on high rise and releasing the convict on probation would not have deterrent effect in the society. Considering the totality of circumstances, convict is sentenced to simple imprisonment till the rising of the court and is further ordered to pay compensation to the complainant for an amount of Rs.4,76,000/- (Rs. Four lakh seventy six thousand only) under Section 357(3) Cr. P.C. In default of payment of compensation, convict shall undergo further simple imprisonment for a period of 03 months. Naval Kishore CC No. 4141/2016 Page no. 13 ::2:: At this stage, an application under Section 389(3) of Code of Criminal Procedure has been moved on behalf of the convict for grant of bail to enable him to file appeal against the order. Heard. Perused. Application under consideration is allowed. The aforesaid sentence is suspended for a period of 30 days from today to enable the convict to file an appeal against the order and till then convict is admitted on bail on furnishing of personal bond of Rs.30,000/- with surety of like amount. Requisite bail bonds furnished. Same are accepted till 26.11.2018. Copy of this order be given to the convict free of cost.
